title: Findmypast, swept
eyebrow: 644 records · 44 record sets · four spellings · 16 September 2026
dek: What a month's full subscription reaches that two expiring trials could not, and the two threads it opened.
lead:
David took a **one-month full subscription** on 16 September 2026. Every earlier pass ran against a clock — the trial of 9 September and the one that lapsed on 14 September, sixteen rows between them on [the search register](/searched/), both ending with a note about reading transcripts before the trial died.

This is the first sweep with no clock on it. **Four spellings, 644 distinct records, 44 record sets** — six more sets than the trials could see, because a subscription opens collections a trial does not.

**The index rows are not the point.** An index row gives a name and a year. A transcript gives parents, a parish, a ship, a street. The transcripts read below are where the two findings on this page came from.
spellings: **the same corpus** — Findmypast folds the space; fourteen pages of it added one record
the same corpus as the fused form; added nothing
**a checked negative.** The spelling exists in this archive's roster and Findmypast has nobody under it
rule: Published only where the person was born before 1930 or a death is on record. **The UK Electoral Registers, the Social Security Death Index, the obituary notices and the divorce indexes are excluded entirely** — they are where the living are, and this archive publishes a living person's name and town and nothing else. 424 of the 644 pass; 220 are counted here and published nowhere.

findings.h: A De Franceschi married a Cosulich in Cardiff in 1876
findings.t:
**Wales Roman Catholic Marriages.** *Emerico De Franceschi*, son of *Francisci de Franceschi*, married *Mariettam Cosulich*, daughter of *Josephi Francisci Cosulich*, at **St Peter's, Roath, Cardiff, on 26 July 1876** — the names in the Latin genitive the priest wrote them in.

**Cosulich is not a name that turns up by accident.** It is one of the great shipowning families of the Austrian Littoral — Lussinpiccolo and Trieste, and in time the Cosulich Line. And Cardiff in 1876 is the coal port of the world, where the Adriatic sailing fleet went to load. Two Austrian-Adriatic maritime families marrying in a Catholic church in a Welsh coal port is [the sea](/at-sea/), not migration.

Nothing yet joins Emerico to this archive's own people. But it is the **first record of the name in Wales**, and it sits exactly where the Lloyd's List work already pointed.

**And it is orderable.** Marietta Cosulich appears exactly once in the whole of Findmypast — this marriage — and the second entry for it is the **civil** register, not the parish one: *England & Wales Marriages*, **Cardiff district, Q3 1876, volume 11A, page 428**, where the GRO clerk read his name as «Emmerico Defrancrschi». The certificate behind that reference gives both ages, both residences, both occupations and the witnesses. **If Emerico is a master or a mate, his occupation joins this marriage to the Lloyd's List work outright.** [Written up as an errand](/errands/).
findings.next: Order the GRO certificate — Cardiff Q3 1876, 11A 428. Then look for Emerico in the Lloyd's registers and in Lussino's parish books.

findings.h: The Puerto Rican cluster is Franceschi, and only its women are visible
findings.t:
**Isabela 11, San Lorenzo 9, Ponce 7**, and after them Guayama, Lajas, Luquillo, Peñuelas, San Sebastián, Yauco, Ceiba and Pueblo Este — **fifty-two records across eleven Puerto Rican towns**, every one of them the **1920 United States census**.

**And every one of them is a woman.** *Filomena Franceschi Dávila de Padilla. Carmen Callejo y Ferrer de Franceschi. Catalina Juliani de Franceschi. Ramona Mato de Franceschi.* Read them in Spanish and the reason is plain: **«de» here is the marital particle, not the Italian nobiliary one.** A woman born Callejo y Ferrer who marries a Franceschi is indexed *de Franceschi*; a woman born Franceschi who marries a Padilla keeps *Franceschi* as her first surname. A search for «de Franceschi» catches every married woman of the family and **not one of its men**, who are filed under plain *Franceschi*.

So the cluster is real and this archive has been looking at it through a keyhole. It is a **Franceschi** family, not a De Franceschi one, and the surname this site is built on is not the surname in it. Nineteenth-century **Corsican** emigration to Puerto Rico is well documented, and Corsica is already here as [a parallel](/corsica/) rather than a connection — which is still the right word for this.

*This page said «a Puerto Rican cluster of the name» when it was first published on 16 September. It is the name minus its particle, and the difference is the whole question.*
findings.next: Search **Franceschi** — not de Franceschi — in Puerto Rico, which is a different and much larger search; then test the given names against the Corsican Franceschi.

findings.h: The Italian parish sets are Naples and Vicenza — a clean negative
findings.t:
Three record sets the trials never opened — *Italy Births & Baptisms 1806-1900*, *Italy Marriages 1809-1900*, *Italy Deaths & Burials 1809-1900* — hold ten records of the name, and **every transcript read puts them somewhere this family is not.**

Two brothers baptised at **San Marco di Palazzo, Napoli** in 1842 and 1844, and a sister born at Napoli in 1855, all three children of *Carmine de Franceschi* and *Angiola Conti*. A *Valentino Mario* born at **Vicenza** in 1900 to Florindo and Angela Torresan. A *Lucia Caterina* born the same year in the frazione **Settecà**, who married at Torri di Quartesolo and died at Vicenza in 1967. A *Domenico*, born 1829 and buried at Vicenza in 1900, son of Carlo and Teresa Facco.

**Napoli and Vicenza. Not Istria, not Carnia, not the Kvarner.** Written down so that nobody opens these three sets again expecting the family in them.
findings.next: Nothing. The set is closed unless a Vicentine or Neapolitan line is ever proposed.

also: **Zdravko Defranceski**, Horsham — the Victorian probate file and the Billion Graves headstone, and **Ruža «Rosa»** beside him, 1996. Both already known; both now have a second source.
**Two burials at River Grove, Cook County, Illinois** in the Chicago Roman Catholic cemetery records — Frieda (1905–1988) and John (1895–1951).
**Seven New York parish records** at named Manhattan churches: Our Lady of Mount Carmel, Ascension, Transfiguration, Our Lady of Pompei, St Joseph on Sixth Avenue, St Anthony of Padua.

**A consular marriage at Smyrna**, 1906–10 — *Eveline L A M De Franceschi*, in the British overseas registers. The candidate spouses Findmypast offers include a **Whittall**, which is the Levantine merchant family of Smyrna. Unresolved, and probably not ours.
**Manuela Campos de Franceschi**, Panama, 1861–1904, and **Antonio Juan de Franceschi Rovo**, Argentina, 1899 — both of whom the [live tree](/live-tree/) also cites, from the same two collections.
how: The session lives in the in-app browser, and on **findmypast.com.au** rather than the .co.uk domain the earlier passes used. The results page is a client-rendered application: its URL wants **«_page»**, not «page», and its own pagination anchors have to be clicked, because a link built by hand triggers a full reload and loses everything gathered so far. Each page yields twenty rows and a transcript id; the id is what the transcript reader takes.
next:
**What this sweep did not do.** The transcripts were read for ten records, not for six hundred — every one of them gives parents, a place and often a note in Italian, and they are the difference between an index and a source. The **images** behind them are a further step again. And the Irish, Scottish and English parish collections have still never been opened under this name.

It is [on the work list](/worklist/), twice: the month, and the map layer these 644 records are going to feed.
